s0003.literal: Huang Faqu; Chunyu Liang; Zhang Zhaoda
s0003.idiomatic: Huang Faqu; Chunyu Liang; Zhang Zhaoda

s0004.literal: Huang Faqu, styled Zhongzhao, was a native of Xinjian in Bashan.
s0004.idiomatic: Huang Faqu, styled Zhongzhao, came from Xinjian in Bashan.

s0005.literal: In youth he was vigorous and swift, brave and strong; on foot he could cover three hundred li in a day and leap three zhang.
s0005.idiomatic: As a young man he was quick and fearless, could march three hundred li in a day on foot, and leap three zhang in a bound.

s0006.literal: He was quite skilled at letters and memorials, clear and adept in registers and accounts; moving in and out of the commandery, the township and hamlets feared him.
s0006.idiomatic: He wrote well and kept accounts with ease. Moving through the commandery, he was feared in every village.

s0007.literal: In Hou Jing's rebellion he gathered followers in his native place.
s0007.idiomatic: When Hou Jing rebelled he raised a band in his home district.

s0008.literal: The Administrator He Xu went down to Jiangzhou; Faqu supervised and managed commandery affairs.
s0008.idiomatic: When Administrator He Xu went downriver to Jiangzhou, Faqu took charge of the commandery.

s0009.literal: The Founder was about to cross the mountains to enter and relieve Jianye; Li Qianshi obstructed him midway; the Founder ordered Zhou Wenyü to encamp at Xichang; Faqu sent troops to aid Wenyü.
s0009.idiomatic: The Founder was about to cross the mountains to relieve Jianye, but Li Qianshi blocked the road. He ordered Zhou Wenyü to camp at Xichang, and Faqu sent troops to join him.

s0010.literal: At that time Faqu had gone out to garrison Xingan county; Jing sent touring commissioner Yu Qing to Yuzhang; Qing divided his troops to strike at Xingan; Faqu resisted in battle and defeated them.
s0010.idiomatic: Faqu was then encamped at Xingan. Jing's touring commissioner Yu Qing reached Yuzhang and sent a detachment against Xingan. Faqu met them in battle and drove them off.

s0011.literal: The Founder also sent Wenyü to advance and campaign against Qing; Wenyü doubted Qing's troops were strong and dared not advance; Faqu led his masses to join him, then advanced and captured Sheng tun, taking captives and booty in great number.
s0011.idiomatic: The Founder also sent Wenyü against Qing, but Wenyü feared Qing's strength and held back. Faqu brought his men to join him, then they advanced together, took Sheng tun, and captured a great host of prisoners and plunder.

s0012.literal: Emperor Yuan of Liang under the provisional mandate appointed him supernumerary fierce general, credentials as Inspector of Jiaozhou, concurrent magistrate of Xingan, enfeoffed as Viscount of Bashan county with a fief of three hundred households.
s0012.idiomatic: Emperor Yuan of Liang, acting under the provisional mandate, made him supernumerary fierce general with credentials as inspector of Jiaozhou, gave him Xingan as magistrate, and enfeoffed him as Viscount of Bashan with three hundred households.

s0013.literal: In the third year of Chengsheng he was appointed bright-prestige general and roaming-cavalry general, advanced in rank to marquis with a fief of five hundred households.
s0013.idiomatic: In Chengsheng year 3 (553) he was made bright-prestige general and roaming-cavalry general, raised to marquis with five hundred households.

s0014.literal: When the Marquis of Zhenyang usurped the throne, he was made left nimble-cavalry general.
s0014.idiomatic: When the Marquis of Zhenyang seized the throne, he was made left nimble-cavalry general.

s0015.literal: When Emperor Jing took the throne, his enfeoffment was changed to Marquis of Xinjian county, fief as before.
s0015.idiomatic: When Emperor Jing came to the throne his title was changed to Marquis of Xinjian, with the same fief as before.

s0016.literal: In the first year of Taiping, four commanderies of Jiangzhou were carved off to establish Gaozhou; Faqu was made credential-holder, scattered-cavalry regular attendant, area commander of Gaozhou military affairs, trustworthy-martial general, and Inspector of Gaozhou, garrisoned at Bashan.
s0016.idiomatic: In Taiping year 1 (556) four Jiangzhou commanderies were split off as Gaozhou. Faqu was made credential-holder and scattered-cavalry regular attendant, commander of Gaozhou armies, trustworthy-martial general, and inspector of Gaozhou, with his seat at Bashan.

s0017.literal: Xiao Bo sent Ouyang Bao to attack Faqu; Faqu fought him and defeated him.
s0017.idiomatic: Xiao Bo sent Ouyang Bao against him. Faqu met him in battle and broke his force.

s0018.literal: In the second year of Yongding, Wang Lin sent Li Xiaoqin, Fan Meng, and Yu Xiaoxiang to attack Zhou Di and also plotted to capture Faqu; Faqu led troops to aid Di and captured Xiaoxiang and three other generals.
s0018.idiomatic: In Yongding year 2 (558) Wang Lin sent Li Xiaoqin, Fan Meng, and Yu Xiaoxiang against Zhou Di and also meant to take Faqu. Faqu marched to Di's aid and captured Xiaoxiang and two other generals.

s0019.literal: His designation was advanced to declare-steadfast general, fief increased together with the former to one thousand households, and one set of pipes and drums was granted.
s0019.idiomatic: His title was raised to declare-steadfast general, his fief brought to one thousand households in all, and he was given a set of pipes and drums.

s0020.literal: For merit in resisting Wang Lin he was appointed pacify-south general and grand master with golden seal and purple ribbon.
s0020.idiomatic: For holding Wang Lin at bay he was made pacify-south general and grand master with the gold seal and purple ribbon.

s0021.literal: Xiong Tanlang rebelled at Jinkou and killed Zhou Wenyü; Faqu together with Zhou Di campaigned and pacified him—the account is in Tanlang's biography.
s0021.idiomatic: Xiong Tanlang rebelled at Jinkou and killed Zhou Wenyü. Faqu and Zhou Di crushed him—the full account is in Tanlang's biography.

s0022.literal: When Emperor Wen succeeded to the throne, his designation was advanced to pacify-south general.
s0022.idiomatic: When Emperor Wen took the throne, Faqu's title was raised to pacify-south general.

s0023.literal: In the second year of Tianjia, Zhou Di rebelled; Faqu led troops to join area commander Wu Mingche and campaigned against Di at Gongtang.
s0023.idiomatic: In Tianjia year 2 (563) Zhou Di rebelled. Faqu led his men to join area commander Wu Mingche and fought Di at Gongtang.

s0024.literal: When Di was pacified, Faqu's merit was foremost.
s0024.idiomatic: When Di fell, Faqu's merit stood first.

s0025.literal: He was summoned as credential-holder, scattered-cavalry regular attendant, area commander of South Xuzhou military affairs, secure-the-north grand general, and Inspector of South Xuzhou, grand-master status and pipes and drums as before.
s0025.idiomatic: He was summoned as credential-holder and scattered-cavalry regular attendant, commander of South Xuzhou armies, secure-the-north grand general, and inspector of South Xuzhou, with grand-master rank and pipes and drums unchanged.

s0026.literal: Before he took up the appointment, soon he was reassigned as area commander of Jiang and Wu commanderies' military affairs, secure-the-south grand general, and Inspector of Jiangzhou.
s0026.idiomatic: Before he could take office he was reassigned to command the armies of Jiang and Wu, made secure-the-south grand general, and named inspector of Jiangzhou.

s0027.literal: In the sixth year he was summoned as central guard grand general.
s0027.idiomatic: In the sixth year he was recalled as central guard grand general.

s0028.literal: When the Deposed Emperor took the throne, he was advanced in rank to duke and given a crutch.
s0028.idiomatic: When the Deposed Emperor came to the throne, Faqu was raised to duke and given a crutch.

s0029.literal: In the first year of Guangda he went out as credential-holder, area commander of South Xuzhou military affairs, secure-the-north general, and Inspector of South Xuzhou.
s0029.idiomatic: In Guangda year 1 (567) he went out as credential-holder, commander of South Xuzhou armies, secure-the-north general, and inspector of South Xuzhou.

s0030.literal: In the second year he was transferred to area commander of E, Ba, and Wu commanderies' military affairs, secure-the-west general, and Inspector of Ezhou, credentials as before.
s0030.idiomatic: In the second year he was transferred to command the armies of E, Ba, and Wu, made secure-the-west general and inspector of Ezhou, with credentials unchanged.

s0031.literal: In the first year of Taijian his designation was advanced to campaign-west grand general.
s0031.idiomatic: In Taijian year 1 (569) his title was raised to campaign-west grand general.

s0032.literal: In the second year he was summoned as palace attendant and central custodian grand general.
s0032.idiomatic: In the second year he was recalled as palace attendant and central custodian grand general.

s0033.literal: In the fourth year he went out as credential-holder, scattered-cavalry regular attendant, area commander of South Yuzhou military affairs, campaign-south grand general, and Inspector of South Yuzhou.
s0033.idiomatic: In the fourth year he went out as credential-holder and scattered-cavalry regular attendant, commander of South Yuzhou armies, campaign-south grand general, and inspector of South Yuzhou.

s0034.literal: In the fifth year a great northern campaign was launched; area commander Wu Mingche went out from Qin commandery; Faqu was made area commander and went out from Liyang.
s0034.idiomatic: In the fifth year a great northern campaign was launched. Wu Mingche marched from Qin commandery while Faqu was made area commander and advanced from Liyang.

s0035.literal: Qi sent the Prince of Liyang's infantry and cavalry, fifty thousand strong, to relieve the city, Editorial footnote marker 1. and at Minor Xiao they built a fort; Faqu sent Left Guard General Fan Yi with a detachment to Great Xiao to meet them, inflicted a great defeat on Qi troops, and captured all men, horses, and equipment.
s0035.idiomatic: Qi sent fifty thousand infantry and cavalry from the Prince of Liyang to relieve the city. [1] They built a fort at Minor Xiao. Faqu sent Left Guard General Fan Yi with a detachment to Great Xiao, shattered the Qi army, and took all their men, horses, and gear.

s0036.literal: Thereupon they built battering carts and foot warships, raised the rams to press on Liyang.
s0036.idiomatic: They then built battering carts and foot warships and drove the rams against Liyang.

s0037.literal: The people of Liyang in distress pleaded to surrender; Faqu relaxed the siege, then they again held firm; Faqu was furious and personally led his soldiers to assault the city, applying the rams to its towers and battlements.
s0037.idiomatic: The people of Liyang, hard pressed, begged to surrender. Faqu eased the assault and they held firm again. Enraged, he led his men in person to storm the walls and set the rams against the towers.

s0038.literal: A great rain fell as well; the walls collapsed and the city was taken; all garrison troops were put to death.
s0038.idiomatic: A heavy rain fell; the walls gave way and the city fell. Every man in the garrison was killed.

s0039.literal: Advancing to Hefei, they surrendered at sight of the standards; Faqu did not allow his soldiers to plunder; he personally comforted and rewarded them, made covenant with them, and sent them all back north.
s0039.idiomatic: At Hefei they surrendered at the first sight of his banners. Faqu forbade plunder, comforted them himself, made covenant, and sent them all back north.

s0040.literal: For merit he was given additional appointment as palace attendant; his enfeoffment was changed to Duke of Yiyang commandery with a fief of two thousand households.
s0040.idiomatic: For merit he was made palace attendant as well and re-enfeoffed as Duke of Yiyang with two thousand households.

s0041.literal: That year he was transferred to area commander of He and Huo commanderies' military affairs, campaign-west grand general, and Inspector of Hezhou, fief increased by five hundred households.
s0041.idiomatic: That year he was transferred to command the armies of He and Huo, made campaign-west grand general and inspector of Hezhou, with five hundred households added to his fief.

s0042.literal: In the seventh year he was transferred to area commander of Yu, Jian, Guang, Shuo, He, and North Xuzhou military affairs, Inspector of Yuzhou, garrisoned at Shouyang; palace attendant, scattered-cavalry regular attendant, credentials, general, grand-master status, pipes and drums, and crutch as before.
s0042.idiomatic: In the seventh year he was made commander of six provinces—Yu, Jian, Guang, Shuo, He, and North Xu—inspector of Yuzhou, and garrisoned at Shouyang, retaining palace attendant, scattered-cavalry regular attendant, credentials, general's rank, grand-master status, pipes and drums, and crutch.

s0043.literal: In the tenth month of the eighth year he died, aged fifty-nine.
s0043.idiomatic: In the tenth month of the eighth year he died, aged fifty-nine.

s0044.literal: Posthumously made palace attendant, central custodian grand general, and Minister of Works; posthumous name Wei.
s0044.idiomatic: He was posthumously made palace attendant, central custodian grand general, and minister of works, with the posthumous name Wei.

s0047.literal: His ancestors were natives of Jibei but for generations dwelt in the capital region.
s0047.idiomatic: His family came from Jibei but had lived in the capital region for generations.

s0048.literal: His father Wencheng served Liang as a general and rose to fierce-radiance general and Inspector of Liangzhou.
s0048.idiomatic: His father Wencheng served Liang as a commander and rose to fierce-radiance general and inspector of Liangzhou.

s0049.literal: In youth Liang was good at deporting himself, of imposing looks, possessed of capacity and strategy, skilled at bow and horse.
s0049.idiomatic: In youth Liang carried himself well, had a commanding presence, showed judgment and resolve, and fought well from horseback.

s0050.literal: When Emperor Yuan of Liang was Inspector of Jingzhou, Wencheng assigned Liang men and horses and ordered him to serve there.
s0050.idiomatic: When Emperor Yuan of Liang governed Jingzhou, Wencheng gave Liang troops and horses and sent him to serve there.

s0051.literal: He began his career as regular attendant of the Kingdom of the Prince of Xiangdong, and concurrently middle-arms adjutant in the Western Center-General's office.
s0051.idiomatic: He entered service as regular attendant of the Prince of Xiangdong's kingdom and middle-arms adjutant in the western center-general's office.

s0052.literal: He rose through the ranks to staff offices, often holding concurrently middle-arms and direct-arms posts for more than ten years; armor-bearing soldiers filled the prince's establishment.
s0052.idiomatic: He rose through staff posts, often holding middle-arms and direct-arms duties together for more than ten years, until armored soldiers filled the prince's household.

s0053.literal: On the border between Jing and Yong, the southern barbarians repeatedly rebelled; the mountain chief Wen Daoqi had long been a frontier trouble; middle-arms Wang Sengbian campaigned against him but repeatedly fought without success and sent Liang to assist.
s0053.idiomatic: On the Jing–Yong frontier the southern tribes rose again and again. The mountain chief Wen Daoqi had long plagued the border. Wang Sengbian campaigned against him without success and sent Liang to help.

s0054.literal: When Liang arrived, he and Sengbian joined forces, inflicted a great defeat on Daoqi, beheaded the chieftains, and took captives numbering in the tens of thousands.
s0054.idiomatic: When Liang arrived he and Sengbian joined forces, crushed Daoqi, beheaded the chiefs, and took tens of thousands of captives.

s0055.literal: For merit he was enfeoffed as Baron of Guangjin with a fief of three hundred households and appointed Administrator of Fuling.
s0055.idiomatic: For merit he was enfeoffed as Baron of Guangjin with three hundred households and made administrator of Fuling.

s0056.literal: He served in succession as Administrator of Xinxing and Wuning commanderies.
s0056.idiomatic: He served in turn as administrator of Xinxing and Wuning.

s0057.literal: When Jingzhou fell, Liang held and defended Guizhou.
s0057.idiomatic: When Jingzhou fell, Liang held Guizhou.

s0058.literal: Wang Lin held and carved up Xiang and Ying; he repeatedly sent summonses to Liang; outwardly Liang kept dealings with Lin, but separately he sent emissaries by a bypath to return to the Founder.
s0058.idiomatic: Wang Lin held Xiang and Ying and repeatedly summoned Liang. Outwardly Liang dealt with Lin, but in secret he sent envoys by hidden paths to the Founder.

s0059.literal: When the Founder received the abdication, he was appointed credential-holder, scattered-cavalry regular attendant, and pacify-west grand general, given one set of pipes and drums, area commander and inspector as before.
s0059.idiomatic: When the Founder took the throne, Liang was made credential-holder, scattered-cavalry regular attendant, and pacify-west grand general, with pipes and drums and his command and inspectorship unchanged.

s0060.literal: Soon his designation was advanced to secure-the-south general.
s0060.idiomatic: Soon his title was raised to secure-the-south general.

s0061.literal: He was then appointed area commander, secure-the-west grand general, and grand master with golden seal and purple ribbon.
s0061.idiomatic: He was then made area commander, secure-the-west grand general, and grand master with the gold seal and purple ribbon.

s0062.literal: When Emperor Wen succeeded to the throne, his designation was advanced to campaign-south grand general.
s0062.idiomatic: When Emperor Wen took the throne, his title was raised to campaign-south grand general.

s0063.literal: After Wang Lin was pacified he repeatedly requested to come to court; in the fifth year of Tianjia he was summoned as central pacification grand general, Editorial footnote marker 2. regular attendant, grand-master status, and pipes and drums as before.
s0063.idiomatic: After Wang Lin fell he repeatedly asked to come to court. In Tianjia year 5 (564) he was recalled as central pacification grand general, [2] with regular attendant rank, grand-master status, and pipes and drums unchanged.

s0064.literal: The generals under Liang's command for the most part longed for their native lands, Editorial footnote marker 3. and all wished to flee into mountain valleys and would not come to court.
s0064.idiomatic: Most of the generals under Liang longed for home. [3] They meant to flee into the hills rather than go to court.

s0065.literal: Emperor Wen sent Inspector of Xiangzhou Hua Jiao to campaign against the Huang cave-folk on the borders of Hengzhou and also to bring troops to receive Liang.
s0065.idiomatic: Emperor Wen sent Hua Jiao, inspector of Xiangzhou, to campaign against the Huang caves on Hengzhou's border and also to bring troops to escort Liang in.

s0066.literal: In the first year of Tiankang he reached the capital; because of delay on the road he was impeached by the relevant office, stripped of grand-master status, the rest as before.
s0066.idiomatic: In Tiankang year 1 (566) he reached the capital. Because he had lingered on the road the authorities impeached him and stripped his grand-master rank, leaving the rest unchanged.

s0067.literal: In the first year of Guangda one set of pipes and drums was granted.
s0067.idiomatic: In Guangda year 1 (567) he was given a set of pipes and drums.

s0068.literal: Hua Jiao plotted treason; Liang was made credential-holder, campaign-south grand general, and grand commander of the western expedition, in overall command of great ships from Ezhou's Fan Ford to resist him.
s0068.idiomatic: When Hua Jiao rebelled, Liang was made credential-holder, campaign-south grand general, and grand commander of the western expedition, leading great ships from Ezhou's Fan Ford against him.

s0069.literal: When Jiao was pacified, he also reduced Zhou general the Senior Duke Tuo Ba Ding and others.
s0069.idiomatic: When Jiao fell he also forced the surrender of the Zhou general Senior Duke Tuo Ba Ding and his men.

s0070.literal: For merit he was appointed palace attendant, central army grand general, and grand master with golden seal and purple ribbon, advanced in enfeoffment to Duke of Liling county with fief increased by one thousand households.
s0070.idiomatic: For merit he was made palace attendant, central army grand general, and grand master with the gold seal and purple ribbon, and raised to Duke of Liling with one thousand households added to his fief.

s0071.literal: Before he took up the appointment he went out as credential-holder, area commander of South Xuzhou military affairs, secure-the-north general, and Inspector of South Xuzhou; palace attendant, grand-master status, and pipes and drums as before.
s0071.idiomatic: Before he could take office he went out as credential-holder, commander of South Xuzhou armies, secure-the-north general, and inspector of South Xuzhou, retaining palace attendant rank, grand-master status, and pipes and drums.

s0072.literal: In the first year of Taijian his designation was advanced to campaign-north grand general and he was given a crutch.
s0072.idiomatic: In Taijian year 1 (569) his title was raised to campaign-north grand general and he was given a crutch.

s0073.literal: In the third year, for sitting with the Prince of Jiangyin Xiao Jiqing in buying trees from the Liang mausoleums, Jiqing was stripped of office and Liang was stripped of palace attendant.
s0073.idiomatic: In the third year he and the Prince of Jiangyin, Xiao Jiqing, were found to have bought timber from the Liang imperial tombs. Jiqing was dismissed and Liang lost his palace attendant post.

s0074.literal: Soon he was again given additional appointment as palace attendant.
s0074.idiomatic: Soon he was made palace attendant again.

s0075.literal: In the fifth year he was summoned as central guard grand general, Editorial footnote marker 4. palace attendant, grand-master status, pipes and drums, and crutch as before.
s0075.idiomatic: In the fifth year he was recalled as central guard grand general, [4] with palace attendant rank, grand-master status, pipes and drums, and crutch unchanged.

s0076.literal: When Wu Mingche campaigned west, Liang endorsed the undertaking and sent his sixth son Cen at the head of his command to follow the army.
s0076.idiomatic: When Wu Mingche marched west, Liang backed the campaign and sent his sixth son Cen at the head of his own troops.

s0077.literal: When the Huai River region was taken and settled, Liang's enfeoffment was changed to Duke of Shi'an commandery with fief increased by one thousand five hundred households.
s0077.idiomatic: When the Huai region was pacified, Liang was re-enfeoffed as Duke of Shi'an with one thousand five hundred households added to his fief.

s0078.literal: In the sixth year he went out as credential-holder, area commander of E, Ba, South Si, and Ding commanderies' military affairs, campaign-west grand general, and Inspector of Ezhou; palace attendant, grand-master status, pipes and drums, and crutch as before.
s0078.idiomatic: In the sixth year he went out as credential-holder, commander of E, Ba, South Si, and Ding, campaign-west grand general, and inspector of Ezhou, with palace attendant rank, grand-master status, pipes and drums, and crutch unchanged.

s0079.literal: In the seventh year he was summoned as central army grand general and protector-general.
s0079.idiomatic: In the seventh year he was recalled as central army grand general and protector-general.

s0080.literal: In the ninth year, for public-business reasons he was stripped of palace attendant.
s0080.idiomatic: In the ninth year he lost his palace attendant post over a public matter.

s0081.literal: Soon he was again given additional appointment as palace attendant.
s0081.idiomatic: Soon he was made palace attendant again.

s0082.literal: In the tenth year, when Wu Mingche was captured and lost, Liang was given additional credentials as area commander of all land and water military affairs, and concurrently appointed scattered-cavalry regular attendant, area commander of South Yan, Bei, and Qiao commanderies' military affairs, chariots-and-cavalry general, and Inspector of South Yanzhou, the rest as before.
s0082.idiomatic: In the tenth year, when Wu Mingche was taken prisoner, Liang was given added credentials as commander of all land and water forces and made scattered-cavalry regular attendant, commander of South Yan, Bei, and Qiao, chariots-and-cavalry general, and inspector of South Yanzhou, with the rest unchanged.

s0083.literal: In the thirteenth year he was given additional title as left grandee of brilliant service, fief increased by five hundred households, the rest as before.
s0083.idiomatic: In the thirteenth year he was made left grandee of brilliant service with five hundred households added to his fief, the rest unchanged.

s0084.literal: In the fourth month of the fourteenth year he died, aged seventy-two.
s0084.idiomatic: In the fourth month of the fourteenth year he died, aged seventy-two.

s0085.idiomatic: He was posthumously made minister of works.

s0086.literal: Zhang Zhaoda, styled Botong, was a native of Wukang in Wuxing.
s0086.idiomatic: Zhang Zhaoda, styled Botong, came from Wukang in Wuxing.

s0087.literal: His grandfather Daogai was Administrator of Guangping under Qi.
s0087.idiomatic: His grandfather Daogai had been administrator of Guangping under Qi.

s0088.literal: His father Fashang served Liang as an assistant in the Yangzhou deliberations office.
s0088.idiomatic: His father Fashang served Liang on the Yangzhou deliberations staff.

s0089.literal: Zhaoda by nature was unconventional, lightly valued wealth and prized bold spirit.
s0089.idiomatic: Zhaoda was free-spirited by nature, cared little for money, and prized boldness.

s0090.literal: In youth he once met a physiognomist who said to Zhaoda: "Your countenance is very fine; you need but a small blemish, and then you will be rich and noble.
s0090.idiomatic: In youth he met a physiognomist who told him, "Your face is too perfect. You need a small flaw, and then you will rise to wealth and rank.

s0091.literal: " In the Datong era of Liang, Zhaoda was direct attendant behind the Eastern Palace; drunk he fell from a horse and received a small wound at the temple; Zhaoda was pleased at this; the physiognomist said, "Not yet."
s0091.idiomatic: " Under Liang's Datong reign he was direct attendant to the Eastern Palace. Drunk, he fell from his horse and cut his temple. Zhaoda was pleased. The physiognomist said, "Not yet."

s0092.literal: In Hou Jing's rebellion Zhaoda led recruits from his native place to relieve the Terrace City; he was struck by a stray arrow and lost sight in one eye; the physiognomist saw him and said, "Your physiognomy is now excellent; before long you will be ennobled."
s0092.idiomatic: In Hou Jing's rebellion he led home recruits to relieve the Terrace City. A stray arrow blinded one eye. The physiognomist saw him and said, "Now your fate is set. You will soon be ennobled."

s0093.literal: When the capital fell Zhaoda returned to his native place and associated with Emperor Wen; thereby they formed the distinction of lord and minister.
s0093.idiomatic: When the capital fell he went home and fell in with Emperor Wen, and from that day they were lord and minister.

s0094.literal: When Jing was pacified Emperor Wen became Administrator of Wuxing; Zhaoda came leaning on his staff to call on Emperor Wen.
s0094.idiomatic: After Jing fell, Emperor Wen became administrator of Wuxing. Zhaoda came leaning on his staff to pay his respects.

s0095.literal: When Emperor Wen saw him he was greatly pleased and therefore entrusted him with command of troops, favor and grace surpassing his peers.
s0095.idiomatic: Emperor Wen was delighted and put him in command of troops, favoring him above his peers.

s0096.literal: When the Founder campaigned against Wang Sengbian he ordered Emperor Wen to return to Changcheng to gather troops and supplies against Du Kan, and repeatedly sent Zhaoda to Jingkou to receive and carry out plans.
s0096.idiomatic: When the Founder moved against Wang Sengbian he sent Emperor Wen back to Changcheng to raise men and stores against Du Kan and repeatedly sent Zhaoda to Jingkou to carry his orders.

s0097.literal: After Sengbian was executed Kan sent his general Du Tai to attack Changcheng; Emperor Wen resisted him and ordered Zhaoda to take overall charge of troops within the city.
s0097.idiomatic: After Sengbian was killed, Kan sent Du Tai against Changcheng. Emperor Wen held the city and put Zhaoda in charge of the garrison.

s0098.literal: When Du Tai withdrew, he followed Emperor Wen eastward; the army was at Wuxing to campaign against Du Kan.
s0098.idiomatic: When Du Tai withdrew, he followed Emperor Wen east. The army camped at Wuxing to attack Du Kan.

s0099.literal: When Kan was pacified he again followed Emperor Wen east to campaign against Zhang Biao at Kuaiji and captured it.
s0099.idiomatic: When Kan fell he marched east again with Emperor Wen against Zhang Biao at Kuaiji and took the city.

s0100.literal: For accumulated merit he was appointed bright-prestige general and Inspector of Dingzhou.
s0100.idiomatic: For accumulated merit he was made bright-prestige general and inspector of Dingzhou.
